harmonicFunction: G9 (I9) - Dominant tonic chord with lush 9th extension (A) establishing the slow jazz blues foundation
C9 (IV9) - Subdominant 9th chord moving to the 4-chord on bar 2, characteristic of quick-change blues
Ab9 (bII9) - Chromatic half-step upper neighbor sliding smoothly into G9 on bar 3
C#dim7 (#IV°7) - Crucial jazz passing chord connecting C9 to G9 with smooth chromatic voice leading (C to C# to D)
Bm7 to Bbm7 to Am7 (iii7 - biii7 - ii7) - Iconic descending chromatic minor turnaround replacing standard static blues chords
D9#5 (V7#5) - Altered dominant chord delivering intense resolution energy pulling back to G9

techniques.name: Chromatic 9th Chord Slides
techniques.description: Sliding movable dominant 9th chord grips down a half-step on the offbeat to create smooth jazz voice leading

notes: Fret the Ab9 chord grip at the 11th fret (or 4th fret) and slide down one semitone into G9
Produces the sophisticated swinging swagger unique to West Coast and Texas jazz-blues
Enables tight harmonic connection without breaking the slow 12/8 rhythm pulse
Fingering: Root on 5th string, 3rd on 4th string, b7 on 3rd string, 9th on 2nd string
Essential vocabulary for any blues guitarist looking to expand into jazz harmony
sequence: Fret G9 at 10th fret of string 5: 10.5 9.4 10.3 10.2
Slide whole grip up one fret to 11th fret (Ab9) on the offbeat
Slide back down smoothly to 10th fret (G9) on the downbeat
Let all 4 chord tones ring evenly without string buzz
Lock into the 12/8 slow triplet swing pulse
tips: Keep finger pressure light during the slide so the fingers glide effortlessly over the frets
Do not lift your fingers off the strings during the half-step slide
Mute the low 6th string with the tip of your middle finger
Use a medium-heavy pick (1.0mm) for warm, round chord attack without clickiness
Listen to T-Bone Walker's original 1947 recording to hear the stylistic origin of the slide
details.progression: Chromatic slide over G9 - Ab9 - G9

techniques.name: 12/8 Slow Blues Comping
techniques.description: Counting four triplet pulses per measure (1-and-a, 2-and-a, 3-and-a, 4-and-a) at an ultra-slow 50 BPM tempo

notes: 12/8 meter gives slow blues its heavy, rolling, rolling-wave dynamic momentum
Chords are generally struck on beats 1 and 3, with subtle rhythmic chops on the eighth-note triplets
Requires immense internal patience not to rush ahead of the 50 BPM tempo
Allows maximum acoustic space between chord attacks for vocal and lead guitar expression
Mastered by the Allman Brothers Band rhythm section (Berry Oakley, Butch Trucks, Jaimoe)
sequence: Set metronome to 50 BPM with triplet subdivision (150 eighth-note clicks per minute)
Strike the G9 chord firmly on beat 1, hold through 'and-a'
Add a soft percussive rake or chop on beat 2
Strike C9 on beat 1 of measure 2 with equal dynamic weight
tips: Relax your shoulders and breathe deeply with the slow 12/8 pulse
Let the chord notes bloom and sustain rather than muting them prematurely
Coordinate with the bass player's walking bassline notes
Keep your chord volume lower than the lead guitar so the solo cuts clearly
Practice playing with minimal wrist tension to sustain the groove over long 8-minute performances

techniques.name: Vocal Microtonal Bends
techniques.description: Slow, emotional string bends with wide finger vibrato emulating human vocal inflections and microtonal blue notes

notes: Slow blues demands bends that unfold gradually over several beats rather than snapping instantly to pitch
The 'neutral third' bend curls the minor 3rd (Bb) halfway up toward the major 3rd (B)
Requires strong wrist rotation and reinforcement with supporting index and middle fingers
Duane Allman's signature technique combining vocal crying bends with singing PAF sustain
Releasing a bend slowly back to pitch creates a heart-wrenching emotional weeping effect
sequence: Fret the 10th fret on the B string (note A) with ring finger, backed by index and middle fingers
Rotate wrist slowly upward to bend the string a full whole step to B
Hold the bent pitch at the peak for two full triplet beats
Apply wide, gentle wrist vibrato at the top of the bend
Release the bend downward with controlled deceleration back to A
tips: Always back up your bending ring finger with your index and middle fingers for stability
Check your bent pitch against a reference fretted note to ensure absolute pitch accuracy
Do not bend with finger muscles alone—the power must come from rotating the wrist and forearm
Turn your guitar volume down slightly (to 8) for sweet overdrive that responds to touch dynamics
Listen to Duane Allman's second solo chorus on At Fillmore East for textbook vocal phrasing

beginner.title: Learn Root-6 and Root-5 Dominant 9th Chords
steps: Master the movable root-5 9th chord shape (used for G9, Ab9, and C9)
Practice sliding from Ab9 down a half-step to G9 in 12/8 time
Form the C#dim7 passing chord grip on strings 4, 3, 2, and 1
Strum through the first 4 bars slowly at 45 BPM with clear note separation
Mute the low 6th string cleanly with the fretting hand during root-5 chords
beginner.goals: Execute clean, buzz-free transitions between G9, C9, and Ab9 chord grips

intermediate.title: Internalize the Stormy Monday Chromatic Turnaround
steps: Learn the descending minor 7th sequence: Bm7 to Bbm7 to Am7
Add the altered D9#5 dominant chord on bar 10 with sharp leading-tone tension
Count 12/8 time: 4 triplet beats per measure (1-and-a, 2-and-a, 3-and-a, 4-and-a)
Comp through the complete 12-bar progression without hesitating at 50 BPM
Practice dynamic control, playing softly behind vocal lines and swelling on turnaround accents
intermediate.goals: Comp through the entire 12-bar substitution matrix with authentic 12/8 feel at 50 BPM

advanced.title: Master Microtonal Bends & Vocal Blues Phrasing
steps: Practice slow, controlled whole-step and 1.5-step bends with wide finger vibrato
Blend G Major Pentatonic sweet notes with G Minor Blues grit over the changes
Target chord tones during the Bm7-Bbm7-Am7 turnaround rather than running generic scales
Incorporate call-and-response dynamics between guitar lines and rhythm comping
Perform a full multi-chorus slow blues solo with dynamic arc and emotional storytelling
advanced.goals: Perform an authentic, emotionally captivating slow jazz-blues solo over the full 12-bar form

commonMistakes: Playing standard straight 4/4 blues chords instead of the sophisticated Stormy Monday substitutions
Rushing through the 12/8 slow blues tempo instead of letting the space between notes breathe
Bending out of tune on slow, sustained vocal bends
Using sterile high-gain modern distortion instead of dynamic tube edge-of-breakup saturation
Ignoring the C#dim7 passing chord which provides the essential jazz voice leading
practiceRoutine: 10 minutes: Slow 12/8 metronome comping on G9, C9, and Ab9 chord grips
15 minutes: Turnaround isolation drill: Bm7 to Bbm7 to Am7 to D9#5
15 minutes: String bending intonation drills targeting root (G), third (B), and flat-seventh (F)
10 minutes: Blending major and minor pentatonic scales over the 12-bar backing track
10 minutes: Full playthrough focusing on volume knob dynamic swells and touch sensitivity
focusAreas: Movable dominant 9th and half-step chromatic slide execution
12/8 slow blues triplet subdivision and rhythmic patience
Pitch accuracy on slow emotional string bends
Passing diminished 7th chord voice leading (C9 to C#dim7 to G9)

metronomeWork: Set metronome to 50 BPM with triplet subdivision (150 eighth-note clicks per minute)
Practice 12-bar rhythm comping, ensuring chords strike squarely on beats 1 and 3

Solo over the progression at 50 BPM focusing on musical space and breathing points
